eras.title: From lagoon refuge to trading city
eras.text: Romans fleeing the Huns and Lombards settle the islands of the Venetian lagoon, which stay under Byzantine rule. The communities elect their own doge, move their capital to the Rialto (c. 810) and grow rich trading between Constantinople, the Islamic world and the Frankish West.

eras.title: Mistress of the Adriatic
eras.text: Venice subdues the Dalmatian coast, wins tax-free trade across the Byzantine Empire (1082) and profits from transporting and supplying the Crusades. Its state shipyard, the Arsenal, is founded.

eras.title: A maritime empire
eras.text: Venice diverts the Fourth Crusade to Constantinople (1204) and takes Crete and a chain of Greek ports. A closed aristocracy rules the city after 1297. It fights a long rivalry with Genoa, loses half its people to the Black Death and wins the War of Chioggia (1381).

eras.title: Wealth, the mainland and the Ottomans
eras.text: Venice's galley convoys carry spices from Alexandria and Beirut to northern Europe. It conquers Padua, Verona, Brescia and Bergamo on the Italian mainland, while losing Aegean bases to the rising Ottoman Empire.

eras.title: Splendour and slow decline
eras.text: Venice survives the League of Cambrai (1508–16) and enjoys the age of Titian, Tintoretto and Palladio, but trade shifts to the Atlantic. It loses Cyprus (1571) and Crete (1669) to the Ottomans despite the victory at Lepanto.

eras.title: Neutrality and the end of the Republic
eras.text: No longer a great power, Venice stays neutral and becomes a highlight of the European Grand Tour. Facing Napoleon in 1797, its Great Council votes the 1,100-year-old Republic out of existence.

eras.title: The Roman Empire in the East
eras.text: After the empire's division, the East — richer and more urban — survives the barbarian invasions that end the West. Justinian I (527–565) codifies Roman law, builds the Hagia Sophia and reconquers Italy, North Africa and southern Spain, but the Plague of Justinian (541) cripples the empire.

eras.title: Survival against Persians and Arabs
eras.text: Exhausting wars with Sasanian Persia are followed by the Arab conquests, which take Syria, Egypt and North Africa. Constantinople survives two Arab sieges (674–78, 717–18) thanks partly to 'Greek fire'. The empire becomes more Greek-speaking and Orthodox; the Iconoclasm controversy splits it over the use of religious images.

eras.title: The Macedonian revival
eras.text: Under the Macedonian dynasty Byzantium recovers: it retakes Crete, Cyprus and Antioch, converts the Bulgarians, Serbs and Rus' to Orthodoxy, and Basil II 'the Bulgar-Slayer' (976–1025) destroys the Bulgarian Empire. Constantinople is the largest and richest city in Christendom, trading through Venice with the West.

eras.title: Turks, Normans and Crusaders
eras.text: Defeat by the Seljuk Turks at Manzikert (1071) loses most of Anatolia. Alexios I Komnenos buys Venetian naval help with trade privileges (1082) and appeals to the West, triggering the Crusades. The Komnenian emperors restore stability, but tensions with the Latins grow.

eras.title: Shattered by the Fourth Crusade
eras.text: Crusaders and Venetians sack Constantinople in 1204 and set up a Latin Empire; Venice takes islands and ports. Byzantine successor states survive in Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond. Nicaea's emperor Michael VIII retakes Constantinople in 1261.

eras.title: The last centuries
eras.text: The restored empire is a shadow of its former self, squeezed between Serbs, Bulgarians, the rising Ottoman Turks and the Italian trading republics who control its commerce. By 1400 it is little more than Constantinople and the Morea. The city falls to Mehmed II on 29 May 1453.

eras.title: From frontier emirate to Balkan power
eras.text: Osman's small Turkish principality in north-west Anatolia expands at Byzantine expense, crosses into Europe (1354) and conquers much of the Balkans after Kosovo (1389). Defeat by Timur at Ankara (1402) nearly destroys it.

eras.title: Recovery and the road to Constantinople
eras.text: After a decade of civil war the sultans rebuild their power, fighting Venice, Hungary and crusading armies (Varna, 1444). Mehmed II takes Constantinople in 1453 and makes it his capital.

eras.title: Superpower
eras.text: Mehmed the Conqueror, Selim the Grim and Suleiman the Magnificent conquer Serbia, Egypt, Syria, Arabia's holy cities, Iraq, Hungary and North Africa. The Ottomans besiege Vienna (1529) and dominate the Mediterranean, taking Venetian islands one after another. Istanbul is the greatest city in Europe.

eras.title: Stability, then setbacks
eras.text: Cyprus is taken from Venice (1571) despite defeat at Lepanto, and Crete after the 25-year siege of Candia (1669). Under the Köprülü grand viziers the empire revives, but the failed siege of Vienna (1683) leads to a disastrous war; by the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) Hungary is lost.

eras.title: Retreat and reform
eras.text: The empire wins back the Morea from Venice (1715–18) but loses wars to Russia and Austria; the Crimea goes to Russia (1783). Serbia and Greece break away. Sultan Mahmud II destroys the Janissaries (1826) and begins Westernising reforms.

eras.title: The 'sick man of Europe'
eras.text: The Tanzimat reforms modernise law and administration, but nationalism, debt and great-power pressure chip away at the empire. It loses most of its Balkan lands (1878, 1912–13), joins the First World War on Germany's side, and is partitioned after defeat. The sultanate is abolished in 1922.

eras.title: Emperors and popes
eras.text: German kings crowned emperor in Rome — the Ottonians, Salians and Hohenstaufen — rule Germany, Burgundy and northern Italy. They clash with the papacy over who appoints bishops (the Investiture Controversy) and with the Lombard cities, which defeat Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano (1176).

eras.title: A patchwork of princes
eras.text: After the Hohenstaufen fall, imperial power weakens; princes, bishops and free cities become nearly independent. The Golden Bull of 1356 fixes seven prince-electors to choose the emperor. The Hanseatic League dominates northern trade; Bohemia is shaken by the Hussite Wars.

eras.title: Habsburg emperors and the Reformation
eras.text: The imperial title passes almost permanently to the Habsburgs. Charles V (1519–56) rules Spain, the Netherlands and the Americas as well — and faces Luther's Reformation. The empire splits into Catholic and Protestant states, and the Thirty Years' War (1618–48) devastates Germany.

eras.title: A loose federation
eras.text: After Westphalia the empire is a loose federation of over 300 states. Austria and the rising Kingdom of Prussia compete for leadership. Napoleon's victories lead Francis II to dissolve the empire in 1806 — as Voltaire joked, it was 'neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire'.

eras.title: The Franks
eras.text: Clovis unites the Franks and converts to Catholicism; the Merovingian kingdom is replaced by the Carolingians, whose Charlemagne is crowned emperor in 800. After the Treaty of Verdun (843) West Francia slowly becomes France, ravaged by Viking raids.

eras.title: The Capetian kings
eras.text: Hugh Capet's descendants slowly expand royal power from Paris. Philip II Augustus takes Normandy from the English kings (1204); Louis IX (St Louis) leads crusades. Gothic cathedrals rise and the University of Paris becomes Europe's intellectual centre.

eras.title: The Hundred Years' War
eras.text: English kings claim the French throne. France suffers crushing defeats (Crécy, Poitiers, Agincourt) and the Black Death, until Joan of Arc's victories (1429) turn the tide. By 1453 the English hold only Calais.

eras.title: Renaissance kings and Wars of Religion
eras.text: A strengthened monarchy invades Italy (1494) and fights the Habsburgs for decades. Francis I brings Leonardo to France. From 1562 Catholic–Huguenot civil wars tear the country apart, including the St Bartholomew's Day massacre (1572).

eras.title: Absolute monarchy
eras.text: Henry IV grants tolerance (Edict of Nantes, 1598). Under Richelieu and then Louis XIV, the 'Sun King' (1643–1715), France becomes Europe's dominant power, ruling from Versailles. Costly wars and debts mount through the 18th-century Enlightenment.

eras.title: Revolution and Napoleon
eras.text: The French Revolution abolishes feudalism and the monarchy (1792), executes Louis XVI and fights much of Europe. Napoleon seizes power (1799), crowns himself emperor (1804) and conquers most of Europe — including ending the Republic of Venice — before final defeat at Waterloo.

eras.title: Monarchies, empire and republic
eras.text: France alternates between restored kings, revolutions (1830, 1848), Napoleon III's Second Empire and, after defeat by Prussia (1871), the Third Republic. It builds the world's second-largest colonial empire in Africa and Indochina.

eras.title: World wars and Europe
eras.text: France bears the brunt of the Western Front in WWI and is occupied by Germany in WWII. After 1945 it loses its empire (Indochina, Algeria), founds the Fifth Republic under de Gaulle (1958) and becomes a core founder of the European Union.

eras.title: Anglo-Saxons and Vikings
eras.text: Angles, Saxons and Jutes settle post-Roman Britain and form kingdoms such as Wessex, Mercia and Northumbria. Viking invasions are resisted by Alfred the Great, whose heirs unite England in the 10th century.

eras.title: Norman and Plantagenet England
eras.text: William the Conqueror's Normans take over England. Their Plantagenet successors rule an empire stretching into France, are forced to accept Magna Carta (1215), develop Parliament, fight the Hundred Years' War and then each other in the Wars of the Roses.

eras.title: The Tudors
eras.text: Henry VII ends the civil wars. Henry VIII breaks with Rome (1534) and Elizabeth I's England defeats the Spanish Armada (1588), begins overseas voyages and enjoys the age of Shakespeare.

eras.title: Stuarts, civil war and revolution
eras.text: The Stuart kings of Scotland inherit England. Conflict between Crown and Parliament leads to civil war, Charles I's execution (1649) and Cromwell's republic, then the Restoration (1660) and the Glorious Revolution (1688). England unites with Scotland in 1707.

names: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

eras.title: Great Britain rises
eras.text: England and Scotland unite (1707). Britain wins naval and colonial supremacy against France, loses the American colonies (1783), begins the Industrial Revolution and leads the coalitions that defeat Napoleon.

eras.title: The Victorian empire
eras.text: Britain is the 'workshop of the world' and rules the largest empire in history — India, much of Africa, Canada, Australia — while its navy polices the seas. At home, railways, reform acts and the abolition of slavery (1833) transform society.

eras.title: Two world wars
eras.text: Britain fights both world wars, standing alone against Nazi Germany in 1940–41. Ireland's southern 26 counties gain independence (1922).

eras.title: After empire
eras.text: The welfare state and NHS are founded; India (1947) and most colonies become independent. Britain joins the European Community (1973) and leaves the EU (2020).

eras.title: Al-Andalus and the Christian north
eras.text: Most of Iberia is Muslim al-Andalus, whose capital Córdoba is the most brilliant city in Western Europe. Small Christian kingdoms in the north — Asturias, León, Castile, Navarre, Aragon — slowly push south in the Reconquista; Toledo falls to Castile in 1085.

eras.title: Castile becomes the great Iberian power
eras.text: After the victory of Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), Castile conquers Córdoba (1236) and Seville (1248), leaving only the Emirate of Granada in Muslim hands. Castile grows rich on wool exported to Flanders and Italy.

eras.title: The Catholic Monarchs and a world empire
eras.text: The marriage of Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon unites Spain. In 1492 they take Granada, expel the Jews and sponsor Columbus. Their grandson Charles V inherits Spain, the Habsburg lands and the Netherlands while conquistadors seize the Aztec and Inca empires.

eras.title: The Golden Age and its decline
eras.text: Philip II rules an empire 'on which the sun never sets', funded by American silver; it wins at Lepanto (1571) but its Armada fails (1588). Spain's 'Siglo de Oro' produces Cervantes, Velázquez and El Greco, but wars and bankruptcies sap its power.

eras.title: Bourbon Spain
eras.text: The War of the Spanish Succession puts a Bourbon on the throne. Napoleon invades in 1808, sparking a brutal guerrilla war and the independence of most of Spanish America. Spain loses Cuba and the Philippines in 1898.

eras.title: Civil war, dictatorship and democracy
eras.text: The Spanish Civil War (1936–39) brings Franco's dictatorship, which lasts until his death in 1975. Spain then becomes a democratic constitutional monarchy and joins the EU (1986).

eras.title: A Mediterranean kingdom forms
eras.text: The small Pyrenean kingdom of Aragon unites with Barcelona (1137). James I the Conqueror takes Majorca (1229) and Valencia (1238).

eras.title: A sea empire
eras.text: After the Sicilian Vespers (1282) Aragon takes Sicily, then Sardinia and, in 1442, Naples, competing with Genoa and Venice for Mediterranean trade. In 1469 Ferdinand of Aragon marries Isabella of Castile, uniting Spain.

eras.title: A kingdom on the edge of Europe
eras.text: Afonso Henriques becomes the first king of Portugal; Lisbon is taken from the Moors in 1147 and the Algarve by 1249. The alliance with England (1386) is the oldest still in force.

eras.title: The Age of Discovery
eras.text: Portugal takes Ceuta (1415) and its captains feel their way down Africa's coast. Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope (1488); da Gama reaches India (1498); Cabral lands in Brazil (1500). A chain of forts from Mozambique to Goa, Malacca and Macau gives Portugal the spice trade — at Venice's expense.

eras.title: Union with Spain, then Brazil's riches
eras.text: Portugal is ruled by the Spanish kings (1580–1640) and loses much of its Asian empire to the Dutch. Brazilian gold funds 18th-century Lisbon, rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake. Fleeing Napoleon, the court moves to Rio de Janeiro (1808); Brazil becomes independent in 1822.

eras.title: Republic, dictatorship and democracy
eras.text: The monarchy falls in 1910. Salazar's Estado Novo dictatorship (1933–74) fights colonial wars in Africa until the peaceful Carnation Revolution of 1974 brings democracy.

eras.title: The popes become princes
eras.text: The Frankish king Pepin gives the pope lands in central Italy (756). The popes rule this territory while fighting emperors over power in Christendom.

eras.title: Avignon, schism and Renaissance popes
eras.text: The popes live at Avignon (1309–77); then rival popes split the Church (1378–1417). Back in Rome, Renaissance popes act as Italian princes, building St Peter's and patronising Raphael and Michelangelo.

eras.title: Counter-Reformation to unification
eras.text: Rome is sacked (1527) and the Church responds to the Reformation at Trent. The Papal States survive into the 19th century, until Italian troops take Rome in 1870. The Vatican City is created in 1929.

eras.title: Venice's great rival
eras.text: Genoa builds a trading empire with colonies in the Crusader states, the Black Sea (Caffa) and Constantinople's suburb of Pera. It fights Venice in four wars, winning at Curzola (1298) but losing the War of Chioggia (1381).

eras.title: The bankers' republic
eras.text: Genoa loses its eastern colonies to the Ottomans but its bankers (the Bank of St George) become financiers of the Spanish Empire. Columbus was a Genoese. The republic ends with Napoleon in 1797.

eras.title: The Visconti
eras.text: The Visconti lords make Milan a powerful duchy (1395) that fights Venice and Florence for control of northern Italy.

eras.title: The Sforza
eras.text: Condottiero Francesco Sforza takes Milan and makes peace with Venice at Lodi (1454). Ludovico Sforza employs Leonardo da Vinci. French and Spanish armies then fight over the duchy.

eras.title: Spanish and Austrian Milan
eras.text: Milan is ruled by Spain until 1714 and then by Austria, until Napoleon arrives in 1796.

eras.title: A merchant republic
eras.text: Florence grows rich on wool, cloth and banking; its gold florin is Europe's standard coin. Dante, Giotto and Petrarch lay the foundations of the Renaissance.

eras.title: The Medici and the Renaissance
eras.text: Cosimo and Lorenzo the Magnificent de' Medici rule behind republican forms and patronise Brunelleschi, Botticelli, Leonardo and Michelangelo. After Savonarola and turmoil, the Medici become Grand Dukes of Tuscany.

eras.title: Normans and Hohenstaufen
eras.text: Norman adventurers conquer southern Italy and Arab-ruled Sicily, creating a rich multicultural kingdom. Emperor Frederick II rules it as a brilliant court in Palermo.

eras.title: Angevins and Aragonese
eras.text: French Angevin kings rule until the Sicilian Vespers (1282) gives Sicily to Aragon. Naples itself passes to Aragon in 1442, and is claimed by France in 1494.

eras.title: Spanish viceroys and Bourbon kings
eras.text: Southern Italy is ruled by Spanish viceroys, then by a Bourbon dynasty (the Two Sicilies from 1816), until Garibaldi's Thousand conquer it for Italy in 1860.

eras.title: The Árpád kings
eras.text: Magyar horsemen settle the Carpathian Basin. Stephen I is crowned the first Christian king (1000). The Mongols devastate the kingdom in 1241–42.

eras.title: A great Central European power
eras.text: Angevin kings and Matthias Corvinus (1458–90) make Hungary a major Renaissance kingdom; it contests Dalmatia with Venice and is Christendom's bulwark against the Ottomans.

eras.title: Divided, then Habsburg
eras.text: After Mohács (1526) Hungary is split between the Ottomans, Habsburg Royal Hungary and Transylvania. The Habsburgs reconquer it by 1699; in 1867 it becomes an equal partner in Austria-Hungary.

eras.title: Independent Hungary
eras.text: Hungary loses two-thirds of its territory at Trianon (1920), joins the Axis, and falls under Soviet control after 1945; the 1956 revolution is crushed. It becomes a democracy in 1989 and joins the EU in 2004.

eras.title: The Piast kingdom
eras.text: Mieszko I accepts Christianity (966). Poland fragments, suffers Mongol raids, and is reunited under Casimir the Great (1333–70). Lithuania, the last pagan state in Europe, expands across Rus' lands.

eras.title: Union with Lithuania
eras.text: Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania marries Queen Jadwiga and converts; the union defeats the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald (1410) and becomes one of Europe's largest states. Copernicus studies in Kraków.

eras.title: The Commonwealth of nobles
eras.text: The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth elects its kings and grants religious tolerance. Jan Sobieski saves Vienna (1683), but a weak central government lets Russia, Prussia and Austria partition the state out of existence (1772–95).

eras.title: Rebirth and survival
eras.text: Poland is reborn in 1918, is invaded by Germany and the USSR in 1939 and suffers enormously, then becomes a Soviet satellite. Solidarity's movement brings democracy in 1989.

eras.title: A crusader state on the Baltic
eras.text: The German crusading order conquers the pagan Prussians and builds a powerful state ruled from Marienburg castle. Its defeat by Poland-Lithuania at Grunwald (1410) begins its decline; in 1525 its last Grand Master becomes the Lutheran Duke of Prussia.

eras.title: Vikings, furs and Constantinople
eras.text: Scandinavian Rus' rulers unite East Slavic tribes along the river route 'from the Varangians to the Greeks'. Vladimir adopts Orthodox Christianity (988); under Yaroslav the Wise Kyiv is one of Europe's great cities.

eras.title: Fragmentation and the Mongols
eras.text: Rus' splinters into rival principalities — Kyiv, Novgorod, Vladimir-Suzdal and others. The Mongols sack Kyiv in 1240 and impose tribute for two centuries.

eras.title: Lord Novgorod the Great
eras.text: A merchant republic governed by its assembly (veche), Novgorod controls a vast fur-producing hinterland and trades with the Hanseatic League. Spared the Mongol sack, it is finally annexed by Ivan III of Moscow in 1478.

eras.title: The rise of Moscow
eras.text: The princes of Moscow collect tribute for the Golden Horde and gradually absorb rival Russian lands. Ivan III ends Tatar overlordship (1480) and annexes Novgorod; Moscow styles itself the 'Third Rome'.

eras.title: The Tsardom
eras.text: Ivan IV 'the Terrible' is crowned tsar, conquers Kazan and Astrakhan and begins the conquest of Siberia. After the Time of Troubles the Romanov dynasty is founded (1613).

eras.title: Peter, Catherine and empire
eras.text: Peter the Great modernises Russia, defeats Sweden and builds St Petersburg. Catherine the Great takes Crimea and much of Poland.

eras.title: Imperial Russia
eras.text: Russia defeats Napoleon (1812), expands into Central Asia and the Caucasus, frees the serfs (1861) and industrialises late. Defeat in war and revolution end the monarchy in 1917.

eras.title: Post-Soviet Russia
eras.text: The Russian Federation emerges from the USSR's collapse. After a chaotic 1990s, Vladimir Putin centralises power; Russia annexes Crimea (2014) and invades Ukraine (2022).

eras.title: Lenin and Stalin
eras.text: The Bolsheviks win the civil war and found the USSR. Stalin's forced collectivisation and industrialisation cause famine and terror, but the Soviet Union bears the greatest share of the fighting against Nazi Germany and emerges a superpower.

eras.title: Cold War superpower
eras.text: The USSR launches Sputnik and Gagarin, dominates Eastern Europe and rivals the USA worldwide. Economic stagnation and Gorbachev's reforms lead to collapse in 1991.

eras.title: Vikings to Kalmar Union
eras.text: Swedish Vikings trade and raid down Russia's rivers. A Christian kingdom forms; from 1397 Sweden is part of the Kalmar Union with Denmark and Norway.

eras.title: Sweden's age of greatness
eras.text: Gustav Vasa makes Sweden independent. Gustavus Adolphus' armies intervene decisively in the Thirty Years' War and Sweden dominates the Baltic, until Peter the Great's Russia defeats Charles XII (Poltava, 1709).

eras.title: Neutral and prosperous
eras.text: Sweden settles into constitutional monarchy, stays out of wars after 1814 and builds a famously generous welfare state; it joined NATO in 2024.

eras.title: Viking Denmark
eras.text: Danish Vikings raid and settle England (the Danelaw); Cnut the Great rules England, Denmark and Norway (1016–35). Denmark dominates the Baltic entrance.

eras.title: The Kalmar Union
eras.text: Queen Margaret unites Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one crown; Sweden breaks away in 1523.

eras.title: Denmark-Norway
eras.text: Denmark and Norway remain united, collecting tolls on all ships entering the Baltic and fighting repeated wars with Sweden. Norway passes to Sweden in 1814.

eras.title: An independent kingdom
eras.text: Kenneth MacAlpin unites Picts and Scots. William Wallace and Robert the Bruce resist English conquest (Bannockburn, 1314). Scotland allies with France and embraces a Calvinist Reformation under John Knox.

eras.title: Union of Crowns
eras.text: James VI of Scotland inherits England (1603). The two kingdoms merge into Great Britain in 1707.

eras.title: Medieval Serbia
eras.text: The Nemanjić dynasty builds a powerful Orthodox kingdom; Stefan Dušan (1331–55) crowns himself emperor. After Kosovo (1389) Serbia becomes an Ottoman vassal and is annexed in 1459.

eras.title: Modern Serbia
eras.text: Uprisings win autonomy and independence (1878). Serbia's conflict with Austria-Hungary sparks WWI; it becomes the core of Yugoslavia (1918–1992), whose violent breakup in the 1990s ends with an independent Serbia.

eras.title: The First Bulgarian Empire
eras.text: Turkic Bulgars and Slavs found a state south of the Danube. It converts to Christianity (864), becomes the cradle of Cyrillic literature and rivals Byzantium, until Basil II conquers it.

eras.title: The Second Bulgarian Empire
eras.text: Bulgaria revives under the Asen dynasty but falls to the Ottomans in 1396, remaining under Ottoman rule until 1878.

eras.title: Mongol rulers of the steppe
eras.text: Batu Khan's western Mongol khanate rules the steppe from the Danube to Siberia from its capital Sarai and collects tribute from the Russian principalities. It converts to Islam under Özbeg Khan. Venetian and Genoese merchants trade at its Black Sea ports of Tana and Caffa.

eras.title: Decline and break-up
eras.text: Civil wars, plague and Timur's invasions weaken the Horde. Moscow defies it, and it splinters into the khanates of Kazan, Astrakhan, Crimea and Sibir.

eras.title: Rome conquers Italy
eras.text: Having expelled its kings, Rome is governed by elected consuls and the Senate. It survives a Gallic sack (390 BC) and conquers the rest of Italy through war and alliances.

eras.title: Mastery of the Mediterranean
eras.text: Rome defeats Carthage in the Punic Wars despite Hannibal's invasion, then conquers Macedon and Greece. By 146 BC it dominates the whole Mediterranean.

eras.title: Civil wars and the end of the Republic
eras.text: Enormous wealth and slave labour bring inequality and political violence. Generals — Marius, Sulla, Pompey, Caesar — use their armies to seize power. After Caesar's murder, Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra and becomes Augustus.

eras.title: The Pax Romana
eras.text: Augustus and his successors rule an empire of perhaps 60 million people from Britain to Mesopotamia. Roads, cities, aqueducts and law spread Roman culture; trade reaches India and, indirectly, Han China.

eras.title: Crisis of the third century
eras.text: Plague, civil wars, invasions by Goths and Persians and runaway inflation nearly break the empire; over 20 emperors rule in 50 years.

eras.title: Diocletian, Constantine and a Christian empire
eras.text: Diocletian divides rule among four emperors. Constantine embraces Christianity and founds Constantinople (330); by 380 Christianity is the state religion.

eras.title: The fall of the West
eras.text: The Western half crumbles under pressure from Goths, Vandals, Huns and others; Rome is sacked in 410 and 455. In 476 the last western emperor is deposed. The Eastern Roman Empire continues.

eras.title: Archaic Greece
eras.text: Hundreds of independent city-states (poleis) emerge. Greeks found colonies from Marseille to the Black Sea, adopt the alphabet, hold the Olympic Games and compose Homer's epics.

eras.title: Classical Greece
eras.text: Athens and Sparta lead the Greeks to victory over Persia. Democratic Athens has its golden age — the Parthenon, Socrates, Sophocles — before the Peloponnesian War with Sparta.

eras.title: The Hellenistic age
eras.text: Philip II of Macedon conquers Greece; his son Alexander conquers Persia. Greek culture spreads from Egypt to Afghanistan in the kingdoms of his successors, until Rome absorbs them.

eras.title: Charlemagne's empire
eras.text: The Carolingians replace the Merovingian kings. Charlemagne conquers the Lombards, Saxons and Avars, is crowned emperor in 800 and sponsors a revival of learning. His grandsons divide the empire in 843.

eras.title: The Migration Period
eras.text: Germanic peoples — Goths, Vandals, Franks, Burgundians, Lombards — cross into the Roman Empire, often as allies and soldiers, and carve out kingdoms on its ruins: the Visigoths in Spain, the Vandals in North Africa, the Ostrogoths and then Lombards in Italy.

eras.title: Successor kingdoms
eras.text: The Visigothic kingdom of Spain lasts until the Arab conquest of 711; the Lombards rule much of Italy until Charlemagne conquers them in 774.

eras.title: Iron Age Celts
eras.text: Celtic-speaking peoples of the Hallstatt and La Tène cultures spread across Europe from Ireland to Anatolia, sacking Rome (390 BC) and Delphi (279 BC). Caesar conquers Gaul by 50 BC.

eras.title: The Celtic fringe
eras.text: Celtic languages and kingdoms survive in Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Cornwall and Brittany, where Irish monks preserve learning in the early Middle Ages.

eras.title: The Huns
eras.text: Nomads from the steppe, the Huns push the Goths into the Roman Empire. Under Attila (434–453) they extort gold from Constantinople and invade Gaul and Italy before their empire collapses.

eras.title: The Habsburg lands
eras.text: The Habsburgs rule Austria from 1282 and through marriages gather Bohemia, Hungary and more; they hold the imperial crown, resist the Ottomans at Vienna (1529, 1683) and fight Prussia under Maria Theresa.

eras.title: The Austrian Empire
eras.text: Francis I takes the title Emperor of Austria. After 1815 Austria rules Venice and Lombardy, and Metternich leads conservative Europe, but revolutions (1848) and defeats lose its Italian lands.

eras.title: Austria-Hungary
eras.text: The 'Dual Monarchy' of Franz Joseph is a multinational empire of Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Croats and others — and the Vienna of Freud, Klimt and Mahler. Its war on Serbia starts WWI; it breaks apart in 1918.

eras.title: Republic of Austria
eras.text: A small German-speaking republic is annexed by Nazi Germany (1938), occupied after the war, and regains full independence as a neutral state in 1955.

eras.title: Duchy to great power
eras.text: The Teutonic Order's lands become the Duchy of Prussia, united with Brandenburg under the Hohenzollerns.

eras.title: Kingdom of Prussia
eras.text: Frederick the Great's army makes Prussia a great power. After defeat by Napoleon it reforms, and under Bismarck it defeats Austria and France to unite Germany.

eras.title: Imperial Germany
eras.text: The new German Empire becomes Europe's industrial powerhouse and acquires colonies in Africa and the Pacific. Its rivalry with Britain and alliance with Austria-Hungary help bring on WWI.

eras.title: Weimar and the Third Reich
eras.text: The Weimar Republic is undermined by defeat, hyperinflation and the Depression. Hitler's Nazi dictatorship launches WWII and the Holocaust.

eras.title: Divided and reunited
eras.text: Germany is split into a democratic West and a communist East. The Berlin Wall falls in 1989 and Germany reunites in 1990, becoming the EU's largest economy.

eras.title: Liberal Italy
eras.text: The new kingdom adds Venice (1866) and Rome (1870). Millions emigrate. Italy joins WWI on the Allied side in 1915.

eras.title: Fascist Italy
eras.text: Mussolini's dictatorship invades Ethiopia (1935) and joins Hitler in WWII; Italy is invaded by the Allies and fights a civil war.

eras.title: The Republic
eras.text: Italy votes to become a republic and enjoys an 'economic miracle', becoming a founder of the European Union.

eras.title: Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands
eras.text: Rich cloth and trading cities like Bruges, Ghent and Antwerp pass to Burgundy and then the Habsburgs.

eras.title: The Dutch Golden Age
eras.text: The northern provinces revolt against Spain and form the Dutch Republic. Amsterdam becomes the world's trading hub; the VOC seizes the spice trade; Rembrandt and Vermeer paint.

eras.title: The Old Swiss Confederacy
eras.text: Alpine cantons ally against the Habsburgs; Swiss pikemen become Europe's most feared mercenaries. Independence is recognised in 1648.

eras.title: Neutral federation
eras.text: Switzerland's neutrality is guaranteed in 1815; it becomes a federal state in 1848 and stays out of both world wars.
